title: Quantifying how environmental viruses control biogeochemical fluxes

concept.text: The innovation would be a validated, transferable way to predict how environmental viral infections change the movement and transformation of carbon and nutrients. It would connect particular viruses to their microbial hosts, identify active infection and its timing, and quantify how infection changes host mortality, metabolism, surrounding microbial communities and material flows.

The intended capability spans cellular events and ecosystem consequences. Measurements of infection would inform estimates of how much material enters dissolved pools, particles, microbial recycling pathways or transport out of the observed ecosystem. Predictions would specify the environmental conditions and time periods over which they apply, together with uncertainty. Transfer across marine and terrestrial environments is a proposed goal extending beyond the marine demonstration supplied here.

Viral abundance and genetic inventories contribute information, but determining an ecosystem effect requires connecting them to active biological processes and measured material flows. As a methodological inference, an annotated auxiliary metabolic gene indicates potential function without establishing its expression, its effect during infection or its contribution to an ecosystem-scale flux. The supplied study does not directly test the predictive sufficiency of auxiliary metabolic gene annotations.

significance.text: A transferable framework could make infection-dependent changes in microbial mortality, metabolism and material routing quantitatively constrained inputs to ecosystem models. Its potentially revolutionary contribution would be reliable prediction across biological scales, from infected cells through community responses to carbon and nutrient fluxes. This is a conditional assessment of the proposed capability. The supplied marine study provides a mechanistic foundation, while broader predictive performance remains to be demonstrated.

The direction of a viral effect depends on the pathways it changes. The viral shunt routes material released from infected cells into pools available for microbial recycling. The viral shuttle concerns infection-associated processes that can promote particle formation and vertical transport. Quantifying the balance requires following the fate of material over time. Increased release or particle production alone leaves uncertainty about subsequent recycling, export and storage.

The proposed advance would improve quantitative constraint on viral processes already considered in some ecosystem models. It would make it possible to test when explicit infection dynamics improve forecasts and how much uncertainty they resolve. The supplied article discusses earlier ecosystem modeling of viral effects, so describing viruses as categorically absent from existing models would overstate the gap.

Potential downstream benefits include better climate projections and more informed land-management decisions, conditional on integration with larger models, independent validation and demonstrated decision relevance. A marine bloom result cannot establish the global virome's net climate effect. Extrapolation would require accounting for ecosystem coverage, the fate and persistence of redistributed material, and interactions with other environmental processes.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability in the proposed record is transferable causal prediction of infection-driven flux changes. The supplied evidence connects active infection to modeled carbon consequences within a particular marine system. Establishing the broader capability would require determining which relationships persist across hosts, viral strategies, community compositions and environmental conditions, and where separate models are necessary.

A concrete measurement barrier is connecting virus identity, host identity and infection state at the temporal resolution needed to explain changing fluxes. Single-cell detection of viral messenger RNA supplies one route to identifying active infection. Scaling this approach across diverse hosts and environments would require assessing detection coverage, sampling biases and the relationship between observed infection markers and subsequent biological outcomes.

Causal attribution is another barrier. Infection levels can vary alongside host physiology, bloom development and community composition. Naturally differing infection levels provide informative contrasts, but extracting an infection-specific effect requires explicit assumptions and control of competing explanations. In the supplied study, the estimate of transparent exopolymer particle production by infected cells depends on the assumption that uninfected cells produce the same amount across enclosures.

Proposed engineering requirements include linking infection measurements to sufficiently complete material budgets, separating organic-carbon release from inorganic-carbon production, and tracking downstream recycling and transport. Models would also need uncertainty estimates that incorporate sampling error, imperfect host assignment and assumptions about per-cell production. Generalization to terrestrial systems and nutrient fluxes beyond the supplied carbon example remains a research target whose present-day status cannot be established from this record.

current_state.text: Flora Vincent, Matti Gralka, Guy Schleyer and colleagues published a relevant demonstration in Nature Communications on 31 January 2023. They studied coccolithophore blooms in seven marine enclosures, combining daily biological and biogeochemical monitoring with infection measurements and modeling. The system provided a concrete connection between host infection, microbial community dynamics and carbon processing during blooms.

The researchers used single-molecule fluorescence in situ hybridization, or smFISH, to detect viral messenger RNA in individual Emiliania huxleyi cells and distinguish actively infected cells. They combined infection measurements with models to estimate population-level and per-cell changes in extracellular carbon production. The modeled components included transparent exopolymer particles, abbreviated TEP, and particulate inorganic carbon, abbreviated PIC. These components represent different carbon forms and require separate interpretation.

The estimates used naturally differing infection levels across enclosures and depended on model assumptions. For example, attributing TEP production to infected cells assumed equal production by uninfected cells across bags. The study therefore demonstrates an approach for estimating infection-associated carbon consequences within its experimental setting. Transferable prediction across ecosystems, independently validated flux forecasts and a global net climate effect remain beyond the demonstrated scope described in the supplied review. Enhanced vertical export was discussed as a potential consequence.

The supplied review assessed the article's main Introduction, Results, Discussion and Methods. The retained extraction was truncated near the final supplementary-material listing, and numerical figures and linked supplementary data were not independently inspected in that review. These limitations constrain verification of detailed effect sizes and supporting analyses. The seven-enclosure scope and qualitative description of the measurement-and-modeling approach are supported by the reviewed main text.

The supplied freshness record is empty. Consequently, the 2023 demonstration can be described historically, while its position relative to later work and the field's unresolved questions as of 1 November 2026 remain undetermined. No later result is established by the supplied materials.

completion_criteria.text: A proposed convincing demonstration would combine host-resolved active-infection measurements with perturbations or well-characterized natural experiments and isotope tracing or mass-balance methods. It would quantify infection-associated changes in carbon and nutrient flows across a defined set of marine and terrestrial ecosystems. This is a proposed evaluation framework. The supplied article establishes a marine experimental foundation for linking infection to carbon processing.

completion_criteria.text: Predictions should be evaluated against independently observed flux changes in held-out time periods, locations or experiments, with uncertainty propagated from measurements and model assumptions. A proposed comparison would test whether incorporating viral effects produces useful predictive improvement over otherwise comparable models that omit those effects. The definitions of useful improvement, acceptable uncertainty and representative ecosystem coverage would need to be specified before evaluation.
completion_criteria.label: Predictions should be evaluated against independently observed flux

completion_criteria.text: Reproducibility would require enough methodological detail, data and model specification for independent teams to repeat the infection measurements, reconstruct flux estimates and examine sensitivity to assumptions. Particularly informative tests would challenge assumptions about uninfected-cell production, competing environmental drivers and the downstream fate of released or particle-associated carbon. Independent replication across contrasting conditions would establish the breadth of demonstrated performance.

completion_criteria.text: Practical completion would include explicit boundaries covering host groups, environmental conditions, spatial and temporal scales, and fluxes for which predictions are reliable. Finite tests can demonstrate performance within those boundaries and reveal transfer limits. A complete catalog of every environmental virus is unnecessary for evaluating predictive performance, and finite validation cannot establish literal universality.

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis connects MIC-11 most closely to MIC-02, A predictive theory of microbial communities. Both seek predictive understanding of community dynamics. MIC-11 concentrates on how viral infection changes material flows and would contribute infection-dependent mechanisms and constraints to broader community theory. MIC-10, Programmable microbial consortia for durable ecosystem functions, shares an interest in ecosystem outcomes. Its engineering objective would draw on understanding viral effects when assessing the stability and performance of designed communities.

MIC-03, Routine experimental access to microbial dark matter, could expand access to poorly characterized hosts and their viruses, improving the coverage of infection measurements. MIC-06, A predictive whole-cell model for microbial design, overlaps through the challenge of predicting infection-associated metabolic changes within cells. MIC-11 additionally requires connecting cellular changes to community interactions and ecosystem material budgets.

MIC-05, A general platform for targeted, adaptable phage treatment, overlaps in virus–host matching and infection dynamics, with treatment efficacy providing its principal application. MIC-09, Forecasting horizontal gene transfer and resistance spread in microbial communities, intersects where viruses participate in gene movement or alter community composition. Its central outputs concern gene and resistance spread, while MIC-11 focuses on carbon and nutrient fluxes.

MIC-04, Reliable nitrogen-fixing microbial partnerships for major cereal crops, shares an interest in nutrient transformations and possible land-management applications. Viral effects on the relevant microbial populations could become one influence on partnership performance, although the supplied marine study establishes no such agricultural result. MIC-12, A causal map from microbial metabolites to host phenotypes, shares the methodological need to connect microbial activity to downstream effects. Its host-phenotype focus gives it a different endpoint from ecosystem flux accounting.

MIC-01, An autonomously reproducing cell built from defined components, could support controlled studies of cellular processes, but its central completion target concerns constructing a reproducing cell. MIC-07, Programmable, reversible living therapies in the human microbiome, and MIC-08, Broadly effective control of bacterial antibiotic persistence, share microbial physiology and community context with MIC-11. Their therapeutic and antibiotic-response objectives remain distinct entries with separate demonstrations of success.

unresolved_issues: The supplied materials do not establish developments after the 2023 study or whether the broad capability remained unresolved as of 1 November 2026.
Numerical figures and linked supplementary data were not independently inspected in the supplied review. Detailed effect sizes, uncertainty estimates and sensitivity analyses remain unverified here.
Representative marine and terrestrial coverage, useful predictive improvement and acceptable uncertainty require operational definitions for a future demonstration.
Transferability beyond the studied coccolithophore blooms, including terrestrial environments and nutrient fluxes beyond the supplied carbon example, remains unestablished by this evidence.
The net contribution of infection-associated recycling, particle production and export to long-term carbon storage and global climate effects remains unquantified in the supplied record.
